# Discrete Spin Structures and the Dimer Model on Surfaces with Boundary

In a previous paper, the authors established a fundamental correspondence between combinatorial and geometric structures on surfaces. Specifically, they demonstrated that certain edge orientations of a graph embedded in a closed oriented surface correspond precisely to discrete spin structures on that surface. This result bridged the gap between the discrete, combinatorial setting of graphs and the more classical, geometric notion of spin structures, revealing that these seemingly distinct concepts encode equivalent information.

This correspondence proved to be more than a structural curiosity; it served as the foundation for a geometric proof of the Pfaffian formula for the partition function of the dimer model. By interpreting edge orientations as discrete spin structures, the authors were able to give a conceptually transparent derivation of this formula, illuminating the geometric principles underlying the combinatorics of dimer configurations.

The present article extends and generalizes these earlier results by moving beyond closed surfaces to the more general setting of compact oriented surfaces with boundary. This generalization is significant, as the introduction of boundaries substantially enriches the theory and opens the door to new operations and interpretations that are absent in the closed case.

A central contribution of this work is a detailed analysis of how cutting and gluing operations act on discrete spin structures. The authors describe precisely how these topological operations—which decompose a surface into simpler pieces or assemble it from constituent parts—transform the associated discrete spin structures. Furthermore, they show how these operations affect the partition function of the dimer model, providing explicit rules that govern its behavior under cutting and gluing.

These cutting and gluing operations carry deep structural consequences. In particular, they enable the dimer model to be reformulated as a quantum field theory on surface graphs. Within this framework, the local operations of cutting and gluing correspond to the compositional structure characteristic of quantum field theories, where physical quantities associated with composite systems are obtained by combining those of their constituent parts. This reformulation situates the dimer model within a broader theoretical context and highlights the rich interplay between statistical mechanics, topology, and quantum field theory.

# The Dimer Model on Surfaces with Boundary: Cutting, Gluing, and a Field-Theoretic Reformulation

The dimer model, a classical object of study in statistical mechanics, describes the statistics of perfect matchings on a graph. When the underlying graph is embedded in a closed oriented surface, a rich interplay emerges between the combinatorial data of the model and the topological and geometric structure of the surface. A central achievement of prior work in this area has been the identification of edge orientations—specifically, so-called Kasteleyn orientations—with discrete analogues of spin structures on the surface. This correspondence provides a conceptual foundation for the celebrated Pfaffian formula, which expresses the partition function of the dimer model as a signed sum of Pfaffians indexed by these discrete spin structures. In this way, the enumeration of dimer configurations becomes tightly bound to the topology of the ambient surface, and the sum over spin structures acquires a precise combinatorial meaning.

The present article builds directly on this body of work, extending the theory from closed oriented surfaces to the more general setting of compact oriented surfaces with boundary. This generalization is far from a routine exercise: the presence of boundary components introduces new features, both in the structure of the graphs under consideration and in the behavior of the discrete spin structures defined upon them. We develop the appropriate framework for edge orientations and Kasteleyn theory in this boundary setting, and we establish the analogue of the Pfaffian formula for the partition function. In doing so, we clarify how the boundary data must be incorporated into the combinatorial and topological description of the model.

A principal contribution of this work is a systematic analysis of the operations of cutting and gluing surfaces along their boundaries. These operations are fundamental to the topological study of surfaces, allowing one to decompose complicated surfaces into simpler pieces and to reassemble them in controlled ways. We examine in detail how such cutting and gluing operations act on discrete spin structures, tracking the way in which these structures decompose and recombine, and we determine the corresponding effect on the partition function of the dimer model. The result is a set of compatibility rules that describe the model's behavior under the manipulation of its underlying surface.

These structural results have a striking conceptual consequence. Because the dimer model on surfaces with boundary behaves coherently under cutting and gluing—assigning to each surface a suitable state space along its boundary and to each cobordism between boundaries a corresponding linear map—it can be reformulated in the language of quantum field theory. In this reformulation, the surfaces and their boundaries play the role of spacetime and its spatial slices, while the gluing axioms mirror the functorial structure characteristic of topological and functorial quantum field theories. The dimer model thus emerges as a quantum field theory defined on surface graphs, in which the partition functions and boundary states fit together according to the rules dictated by the topology of the surfaces.

This field-theoretic perspective offers a new and unifying framework for understanding the dimer model. It reorganizes known results about partition functions and spin structures into a compositional structure, revealing how local combinatorial data assemble into global topological invariants. Beyond providing an elegant reinterpretation of existing formulas, this framework opens the way to new techniques and questions, connecting the combinatorics of dimers to the broader landscape of quantum field theory and the topology of surfaces.

# The Pfaffian: A Central Object in a Mathematical Thesis

## Introduction

The **Pfaffian** stands as one of the most elegant constructions in linear algebra and combinatorics, making it a natural focus for many a mathematical **thesis**. Named after the German mathematician Johann Friedrich Pfaff, this concept bridges the abstract worlds of matrix theory, graph theory, and mathematical physics.

## What Is the Pfaffian?

The Pfaffian is a polynomial associated with a **skew-symmetric matrix** (a square matrix $A$ satisfying $A^T = -A$). Its defining property is remarkable in its simplicity:

$$\text{Pf}(A)^2 = \det(A)$$

In other words, the Pfaffian is a kind of "square root" of the determinant, but one that carries additional sign information. For a $2n \times 2n$ skew-symmetric matrix, the Pfaffian is a polynomial in the matrix entries, while it vanishes identically for matrices of odd dimension.

## Why It Deserves a Thesis

Devoting a **thesis** to the study of Pfaffians is well justified by their extraordinary reach across disciplines:

1. **Combinatorics** — The Pfaffian counts perfect matchings in certain graphs, connecting linear algebra to enumeration problems.

2. **Statistical Physics** — In the study of the Ising model and dimer coverings, Pfaffians provide exact solutions that would otherwise be intractable.

3. **Algebraic Geometry** — Pfaffian varieties, defined by the vanishing of Pfaffians of submatrices, form rich objects of study.

4. **Quantum Field Theory** — Pfaffians appear naturally in the treatment of fermionic systems and Grassmann integrals.

## A Foundation for Research

A doctoral **thesis** exploring the Pfaffian might investigate its role in the **FKT algorithm** (Fisher–Kasteleyn–Temperley), which efficiently counts perfect matchings in planar graphs—one of the few tractable cases of an otherwise difficult computational problem. Alternatively, the work could delve into generalizations, such as the **hyperpfaffian** or connections to the theory of symmetric functions.

## Conclusion

The Pfaffian embodies the deep unity of mathematics: a single object simultaneously algebraic, geometric, and combinatorial. It is precisely this multifaceted character that makes it a rewarding subject for a **thesis**, offering the researcher an inexhaustible source of connections and open questions.

**Dimer Models, Spin Structures, and Edge Orientations on Surfaces with Boundary**

The dimer model on graphs embedded in closed surfaces has a rich combinatorial and topological structure, most notably captured by the correspondence between Kasteleyn orientations of an embedded graph and spin structures on the underlying surface. This connection, developed by Cimasoni and Reshetikhin and others, expresses the partition function of the dimer model as a sum over spin structures of Pfaffians, with signs governed by quadratic forms on the first homology group with $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ coefficients. In this paper, we extend this framework to compact surfaces with nonempty boundary. We introduce a notion of *relative Kasteleyn orientation* adapted to graphs with boundary conditions, and prove that equivalence classes of such orientations are in canonical bijection with *relative spin structures* on the surface, classified by an appropriate torsor over $H^1(\Sigma, \partial\Sigma; \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})$. As applications, we compute partition functions for planar domains and cylinders with prescribed boundary matchings, recovering and generalizing classical results, and we clarify the role of boundary monomers as sources of relative homology classes. Our results provide a unified topological interpretation of boundary effects in the dimer model and open the way toward extensions to open topological field theories and to the study of dimer models on surfaces with corners.

# Introduction

The dimer model, a cornerstone of statistical mechanics since its introduction in the study of adsorption phenomena and its exact solution by Kasteleyn, Temperley, and Fisher in the 1960s, has enjoyed a remarkable resurgence at the intersection of combinatorics, probability theory, and mathematical physics. At its heart, the model concerns perfect matchings of a graph embedded on a surface, whose partition function encodes deep geometric and topological information about the underlying manifold. A central insight of Kasteleyn's original approach—later formalized and generalized through the language of discrete spin structures—is that the signs required to orient the dimer weights consistently are governed by the topology of the host surface. For a graph embedded in a surface of genus $g$, the partition function decomposes as a signed sum over $2^{2g}$ Pfaffians, each corresponding to a distinct spin structure, or equivalently to a class in $H^1(\Sigma; \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})$. This correspondence, made precise through the work of Cimasoni, Reshetikhin, and others, reveals that Kasteleyn orientations are naturally in bijection with discrete spin structures, thereby recasting a combinatorial construction in the framework of geometric topology. In the present article, we develop this perspective further by reformulating the dimer model as a quantum field theory, wherein the sum over dimer configurations is realized as a functional integral over fermionic (Grassmann) fields, and the spin-structure dependence emerges as a choice of boundary conditions for the fermion propagator. This field-theoretic reformulation not only illuminates the origin of the Pfaffian structure and its modular properties under the mapping class group of the surface, but also provides a conceptual bridge to conformal field theory in the continuum scaling limit, situating the discrete model within the broader program of understanding two-dimensional critical phenomena.

We present a unified framework connecting the classical dimer model on graphs embedded in oriented surfaces to the theory of spin structures and a discrete quantum field theory. Building on the foundational work relating dimer configurations to Pfaffians and Kasteleyn orientations, we establish that the partition function of the dimer model decomposes as a signed sum over spin structures on the underlying surface, with each term computed by a Kasteleyn-type Pfaffian.

Our central result identifies the space of Kasteleyn orientations, modulo natural equivalence, with the torsor of spin structures on the oriented surface. This correspondence, which realizes the $2^{2g}$ spin structures on a genus-$g$ surface as distinct sign conventions in the Pfaffian expansion, provides a topological interpretation of the summation formula for the dimer partition function first conjectured in the physics literature.

We further develop a quantum field-theoretic reformulation in which dimer correlation functions arise as expectation values of fermionic observables in a lattice theory of free Majorana fields. Within this framework, the Grassmann integral representation makes manifest the role of spin structures as boundary conditions for the fermionic path integral, and the modular transformation properties of the partition function under the mapping class group emerge naturally. We show that the discrete holomorphic structure on the graph, encoded by the Kasteleyn operator, converges in the continuum limit to the Cauchy–Riemann operator coupled to the corresponding spin structure.

As applications, we derive explicit formulas for the dimer partition function on the torus and higher-genus surfaces, recover known results on the critical behavior and conformal invariance of the model, and clarify the relationship between the combinatorial theory of perfect matchings and the algebraic geometry of the associated spectral curves. Our results provide a rigorous bridge between statistical mechanics, low-dimensional topology, and conformal field theory.
